Mahanadi River Dispute

•On April 20, 2026, the Mahanadi Water Dispute Tribunal (MWDT) issued a
 warning to Odisha and Chhattisgarh, giving them a last opportunity until
 May 2, 2026, to finalize a consensual settlement formula.


•The tribunal, chaired by former Supreme Court judge Justice Bela M. Trivedi,
 expressed displeasure over repeated adjournments and the failure to place any
 concrete proposal on record.


•If the states fail to submit a consensus by the next hearing, the tribunal has
 made it clear that it will proceed to adjudicate the decade-long dispute
 on its merits without further delay.

Mahanadi River Dispute
The Mahanadi River –
•The Mahanadi originates in Chhattisgarh’s Dhamtari district and
 flows 857 kms before entering Odisha, finally draining into the Bay of
 Bengal.


•The river sustains irrigation (2.35 lakh hectares), hydropower (347.5
 MW), and fisheries across at least 20 of Odisha’s 30 districts.


•The Mahanadi has a total catchment area of 1,41,600 sq km, of
 which 53.9% lies in Chhattisgarh, 45.73% in Odisha, and a small
 portion in Madhya Pradesh.

Mahanadi River Dispute

•The current conflict began in 2016 when Odisha accused Chhattisgarh of
 “unilaterally constructing” at least eight barrages along the river.


•Odisha, as the lower riparian state, alleged that these upstream projects
 severely impacted water flow into Odisha, particularly during the non-
 monsoon seasons.


•In response, the Union government attempted to resolve the issue through a
 tripartite meeting with then Chief Ministers Naveen Patnaik (Odisha) and
 Raman Singh (Chhattisgarh), chaired by Union Minister Uma Bharti.

Mahanadi River Dispute
•Odisha’s Argument: The river is a lifeline for its agriculture, power
 generation, and fisheries. Odisha maintains that its historical use and the
 ecological needs of the delta give it a primary claim to the water.


•Chhattisgarh’s Argument: As the upper riparian state with over 86%
 of the catchment area up to the Hirakud dam, it argues it has every right to
 use the river's water for its own industrial and economic development.


•Chhattisgarh further points out that of the 35,308 MCM contributed to
 the Hirakud dam, it is currently using only 9,000 MCM, arguing it has the
 right to utilize more.

Mahanadi River Dispute

•Six biodiversity hotspots, including Bhitarkanika, Chilika, and
 Tikarpada, depend on the river’s flows, making the dispute also an
 ecological matter of national importance.


•The dispute has a direct economic impact, as the Mahanadi is critical for
 irrigation, industry, and power generation. The basin contributes
 nearly 40-45% of India’s industrial steel production.

Mahanadi River Dispute
Constitutional Provisions –
•Article 262(1) of the Constitution empowers Parliament to provide by
 law for the adjudication of disputes relating to the use, distribution, or
 control of waters of inter-state rivers or river valleys.


•Article 262(2) allows Parliament to provide that neither the Supreme
 Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such
 dispute, thus potentially excluding the apex court’s jurisdiction.


•The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act (ISRWD), 1956, was
 enacted under Article 262 to create a dispute resolution mechanism.

Mahanadi River Dispute
ISRWD Act, 1956 –
•Under this Act, when a state government makes a complaint regarding a
 water dispute and the central government believes the dispute cannot be
 settled by negotiations, a Water Disputes Tribunal is constituted to
 adjudicate the matter.


•The Act provides that the decision of the tribunal, after being published in
 the official gazette, shall have the same force as an order or decree of
 the Supreme Court.


•The Act’s provision for creating a separate tribunal for each dispute has
 caused major delays, leading to widespread demands for reform.

Mahanadi River Dispute
National Interlinking of Rivers Project (NRLP) –
•It was formulated in August 1980 to transfer water from surplus basins
 to deficit/deficit basins to mitigate floods and droughts.


•The National Water Development Agency (NWDA) was established
 in 1982 under the Ministry of Jal Shakti to study the feasibility of inter-
 basin water transfer.
•As of 2025, out of the 30 identified links, Pre-Feasibility Reports (PFRs)
 are complete for all 30 projects, Feasibility Reports (FRs) for 26, and
 Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for 13 link projects.

Mahanadi River Dispute
•The 30 links are divided into two major components: the Himalayan
 Component (14 links) connecting the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna
 system, and the Peninsular Component (16 links) for links connecting
 rivers like Mahanadi, Godavari, and Cauvery.


•Five links have been designated as national priority projects: Ken-Betwa
 Link (KBLP), Modified Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (PKC), and a three-part
 Godavari-Cauvery Link.


•The Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP) is the first under implementation,
 approved in December 2021 with an estimated cost of ₹44,605 crore,
 targeted for completion by 2030.

Mahanadi River Dispute
Background of the Mahanadi dispute –
•In December 2016, the Odisha government bypassed the tribunal route
 and directly moved the Supreme Court by filing an original suit under
 Article 131 of the Constitution.


•Article 131 grants the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction over
 disputes between the Government of India and one or more states, or
 between two or more states.


•Odisha’s suit sought an injunction against Chhattisgarh to prevent it from
 constructing further barrages along the river.

Mahanadi River Dispute
•Following the Supreme Court’s directive in January 2018, the Centre
 constituted the Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal on March 12,
 2018, under the ISRWD Act, 1956.


•The tribunal is currently composed of Justice Bela M. Trivedi
 (Chairperson), along with members Justice Ravi Ranjan and Justice
 Indermeet Kaur Kochhar.


•The Commission has powers equivalent to a civil court for
 summoning witnesses and requiring the production of documents, and
 the tribunal’s term has been extended by nine months, pushing its new
 deadline to January 13, 2027.

Mahanadi River Dispute

•The 2017 Amendment Bill proposed to replace the provision for separate
 tribunals with a single, permanent Inter-State River Water Disputes
 Tribunal, with multiple benches for each dispute to speed up adjudication.


•It introduced a Disputes Resolution Committee (DRC) for amicable
 resolution before the matter goes to the tribunal, to be given one year
 (extendable by six months) to submit its report.


•The Bill also reduced the time limit for the tribunal to give its decision from
 three to two years (extendable by one year). However, it remains pending
 in Parliament.

Mahanadi River Dispute
Recent Warning –
•In its April 20 order, the tribunal made it clear that it is “not very
 happy with the manner” in which the proceedings are being
 conducted.
•The bench noted that despite multiple technical committee meetings, the
 states have failed to submit any “concrete proposal for settlement
 on any of the disputed issues”.
•The tribunal observed that the proceedings are being adjourned at the
 order of the parties on the ground that they are “seriously considering
 settlement,” but nothing substantial has materialized.

Mahanadi River Dispute

•On April 11, both states had jointly submitted that the minutes of a
 crucial technical meeting regarding “annual water availability in mean
 annual flow” held on April 8 would be finalized by April 20.


•On the deadline, the respective Advocate Generals again sought more
 time, claiming the meeting data was “crucial”, prompting the tribunal to
 issue its final warning.


•The tribunal fixed May 2, 2026, as the next date of hearing, warning
 that this would be the last opportunity to place a consensus on record.

Mahanadi River Dispute

•The states had submitted a joint request to the Centre, leading to
 an extension of the tribunal’s tenure by nine months till January 13,
 2027.
•The Odisha government formed a high-level committee headed by
 Deputy CM K V Singh Deo, and officials from both states have held
 multiple meetings.
•The tribunal noted that although there are plans by Odisha and
 Chhattisgarh to hold a chief ministers’ meeting to resolve the dispute
 amicably, no consensus has been reached yet.

Mahanadi River Dispute

•The tribunal has made its position clear: if no consensus is placed on record
 by May 2, it will proceed to hear the references on the case’s
 merits and adjudicate the dispute on its own.


•The tribunal’s bench has the authority to frame issues, hear arguments, and
 pass a final, binding award that applies to the sharing of the Mahanadi
 waters.


•If the tribunal adjudicates, it may be years before a final decision is
 implemented, as tribunal awards are often challenged and litigated further.

99th Ramsar Site


• Shekha Jheel Bird Sanctuary in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh, has
  been designated as India’s 99th Ramsar site, bringing the
  country closer to the major environmental milestone of 100 wetland
  sites.

• With this recognition, Uttar Pradesh now has 12 Ramsar sites,
  the highest among all Indian states, further strengthening its
  ecological importance in wetland conservation.

• Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav announced the
  designation, highlighting its benefits for biodiversity, local livelihoods,
  climate security, and water conservation.

99th Ramsar Site

What are Ramsar sites?

• Wetlands are areas where water either covers the soil or is
present near the soil surface throughout the year or for varying
durations, including the growing season.

• The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands defines wetlands as

➢ “areas of marsh, fen, peat land or water, whether natural or
artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or
flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, including areas of marine water the
depth of which at low tide does not exceed six meters”.

99th Ramsar Site


• For the purposes of this classification, wetlands must have one or
more of the following three attributes:

(1) at least periodically, the land supports predominantly
    hydrophytes;
(2) the substrate is predominantly undrained hydric soil; and
(3) the substrate is non-soil and is saturated with water or covered
    by shallow water at some time during the growing season of
    each year”.

99th Ramsar Site


• The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, also known as the
Convention on Wetlands, is an intergovernmental treaty for the
conservation and wise use of wetlands.

• A Ramsar Site is a wetland site designated to be of
international importance.

• These wetlands are protected under strict guidelines of the
Ramsar Convention on Wetlands.

99th Ramsar Site


• The Convention was adopted in the Iranian city of Ramsar in
1971 and came into force in 1975.

• Since then, almost 90% of UN member states, from all the
world’s geographic regions, have acceded to become “Contracting
Parties”.

• This requires international cooperation, policy making, capacity
building and technology transfer.

99th Ramsar Site


• The Contracting Parties meet every three years at a
Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP) to discuss policy
issues.

• They report on the activities of the previous three years through
National Reports.

• The next Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP16) to the
Ramsar Convention on Wetlands is scheduled to take place
in Panama City, Panama, from 7 to 15 June 2028.

99th Ramsar Site


• The Montreux Record is a register of wetland sites on the List
of Wetlands of International Importance and is maintained under
Ramsar sited.

• It includes sites where changes in ecological character have
occurred, are occurring, or are likely to occur as a result of human
interference.

• The Montreux Record was established by Recommendation
4.8 of the Conference of the Contracting Parties (1990).

99th Ramsar Site


• Today, the Ramsar List is the world’s largest network of protected
areas.

• There are over 2,400 Ramsar Sites on the territories of 172
Convention Contracting Parties across the world, covering
more than 2.5 million square kilometres.

• The world’s first Site was the Cobourg Peninsula in Australia,
designated in 1974.

99th Ramsar Site


• The largest Sites are Rio Negro in Brazil (120,000 square
kilometres), and Ngiri-Tumba-Maindombe in Congo.

• The countries with the most Sites are the United Kingdom with
175 and Mexico with 144.

• Bolivia has the largest area with 148,000 square km under
the Convention protection; Canada, Chad, Congo and the Russian
Federation have also each designated over 100,000 square km.

99th Ramsar Site

Ramsar convention in India –

• India is a party to the Convention since 1982 and India was a
  member of the Standing Committee from 1999-2002.

• As of April 2026, India has 99 Ramsar sites, covering a total
  area of approximately 1.38 million hectares, with Shekha
  Jheel being the latest addition.

• Chilika Lake in Orissa and Keoladeo National Park in
  Rajasthan were recognised as the first Ramsar sites in 1981
  in India.

99th Ramsar Site


• India has the largest number of Ramsar sites in Asia and
  ranks third globally after the United Kingdom and Mexico in
  total number of sites.

• Tamil Nadu has the highest number of Ramsar sites (20),
  followed by Uttar Pradesh (12) and West Bengal (8) .

• The Sunderbans (West Bengal) is the largest Ramsar site in
  India, while the Renuka Wetland (Himachal Pradesh) is the
  smallest.

99th Ramsar Site


• Wetlands cover approximately 6% of the Earth’s total land
  surface, providing essential ecosystem services.

• As per the latest national assessments, India's wetlands cover
  approximately 15.98 million hectares (about 4.86% of the
  country’s geographical area), and the total number of wetlands
  is 757,060.

• In India, inland-natural wetlands account for the largest
  share (about 43.4% ), followed by coastal-natural
  wetlands (about 24.3% ) of the total wetland area.

99th Ramsar Site


• India has the largest network of Ramsar sites in Asia and
  ranks third globally, with the network expanding by
  over 250% in the last decade.

• Udaipur (Rajasthan) and Indore (Madhya Pradesh) are India’s
  first cities to be accredited as Wetland Cities under the
  Ramsar Convention.

• India has 19 types of wetlands, as classified by the National
  Wetland Inventory and Assessment (NWIA) under the
  guidelines of the Ramsar Convention.

99th Ramsar Site

Awards -

• The Ramsar Wetland Conservation Awards were
established in 1996 to recognize individuals and organizations
for wetland conservation and wise use.

• The awards were created at the 6th Conference of the
Parties (COP6) in 1996 through Resolution VI.18.

• Recipients receive the Evian Special Prize of USD 10,000,
sponsored by Danone.

99th Ramsar Site

• The awards have been presented six times during Ramsar COP
meetings in 1999, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2012, and 2015.

• There are three award categories:
➢ Wetland Wise Use
➢ Wetland Innovation
➢ Young Wetland Champions

• The Ramsar Wetland Conservation Award for Innovation
recognizes a person, project, program, or policy that has
used an innovative technique or approach for wetland
conservation.

99th Ramsar Site

• The Ramsar Wetland Conservation Award for Young
Wetland Champions honors individuals or groups aged 18-
30 for their work in wetland conservation, wise use, and
restoration.

• The Ramsar Wetland Indigenous Peoples Conservation
and Wise Use Award acknowledges groups or individuals for
leadership and transformative projects involving indigenous
peoples in wetland conservation.

99th Ramsar Site

New site –

• Shekha Jheel is a freshwater lake located 17 km from Aligarh
  city on the Aligarh-Jalali road, near Sheikha and Bhawan-Khera
  villages in Koil tehsil.

• Spanning 25 hectares, the lake is a perennial water
  body formed in 1852 when the Upper Ganges Canal was
  constructed, which flows adjacent and prevents drying.

• The sanctuary hosts 249 bird species, of which 62 species are
  specifically dependent on the wetland ecosystem for survival.

99th Ramsar Site

• It is Uttar Pradesh’s smallest bird sanctuary (only 1 sq km
  wetland), yet hosts nearly 20,000 migratory birds of 186
  species annually, including Sarus Crane, Black-necked Stork, and
  Indian River Tern.

• It is an Important Bird and Biodiversity Area (IBA) by BirdLife
  International and supports three threatened turtle species:
  Black Pond Turtle, Indian Flap-shelled Turtle, and Ganges
  Soft-shelled Turtle.

• Once a hunting ground, it was saved by the Nature Conservation
  Society of Aligarh - the local community now prevents poaching,
  making it a conservation success story.

99th Ramsar Site

Indian Initiatives -

• Protecting existing wetlands and restoring degraded ones is
critical for building climate resilience and ensuring our
survival.

• While Ramsar sites are prioritised for protection, there are
several other urban wetlands which must also be accorded due
importance.

• At the national level, the MoEFCC also implements several
programs and initiatives aimed at conserving and managing
wetlands in the country.

99th Ramsar Site


• The National Wetland Conservation Program (NWCP)
launched in 1985 provides financial and technical assistance to
states and UTs for the preservation and management of wetlands.

• The National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) was approved
by Government of India as 100% centrally sponsored scheme.

• To enhance synergy and prevent overlap, the two schemes were
consolidated into a centrally sponsored scheme called the
'National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Eco-systems'
(NPCA) in February 2013.

99th Ramsar Site


• The MoEF&CC has notified Wetlands (Conservation and
Management) Rules, 2017, under the provisions of the
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

• These rules serve as a regulatory framework for the conservation
and management of wetlands across the country.

• The aim is to conserve, manage, and maintain the ecological
character of the wetlands without restricting their wise use.

99th Ramsar Site


• The Government of India also launched the Amrit Sarovar
Mission in 2022.

• Under the Mission, 75 water bodies will be developed and
rejuvenated in each district of the country as a part of the
celebration of Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav.

• In total, the Mission aims at creating 50,000 water bodies of a
size of about an Acre or more.

99th Ramsar Site


• The Amrit Dharohar initiative, part of the 2023-24 budget
announcement, was launched by MoEF&CC in June 2023.

• The initiative aims to promote Ramsar Sites' unique conservation
values in the country, creating employment opportunities and
supporting local livelihoods.

• Implemented over three years, this initiative involves
collaboration with Central Government ministries, State Wetland
Authorities, and a network of institutions and individuals.

99th Ramsar Site


• World Wetlands Day is celebrated every year on 2 February to
mark the date of the adoption of the Ramsar Convention.

• The theme of WWD-2026 is ‘Water and Gender’.

• The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change
(MoEFCC) organised the main national event at the Asola Bhatti
Wildlife Sanctuary in Delhi – the largest wildlife sanctuary in
the capital.
